title: Take off your shoes
hookLine: at the burning bush, Moses is told the ground is holy (Exodus 3:1–5)

cards: Moses isn't looking for anything. Exodus sets the scene plainly, in the King James words: "Now Moses kept the flock of Jethro his father in law, the priest of Midian: and he led the flock to the backside of the desert".
A shepherd at work, far from anywhere, with someone else's sheep. Then, at the edge of his vision, a bush on fire. The fire isn't the strange part.
The strange part is what it isn't doing.

teach.b: First, the sight. Exodus says "the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed." Fire that doesn't use anything up: a plain thing doing something it shouldn't.
Second, the turn. Moses says: "I will now turn aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt." He leaves the path and stops herding long enough to look.
The next line is the hinge of the story: "And when the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called unto him out of the midst of the bush". In the text, the call comes after the turning aside.
Third, the instruction: "Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground." Notice where the holiness is. Not in a temple.
Exodus calls this Horeb, the mountain of God, but Moses came there with sheep, not to worship: the dirt under his own feet, at his ordinary work. Fourth, the gesture.
Taking off shoes is a way the body says: this place is different, and I'm not in charge here.
In mosques, shoes come off before prayer, and the Qur'an tells the same story, with Moses told to take off his shoes in the holy valley. Some homes ask guests to leave their shoes at the door.
The feet go bare, and the ground can be felt.

how: Muslims remove their shoes before praying in a mosque, and shoes come off in Hindu and Sikh temples too; Jews and Christians read the burning bush in Exodus 3 as the moment Moses is called.

o: the desert town where Moses was born and raised
the valley where the Israelites built a temple
the mountain where Moses took off his shoes

games.q: the burning bush — tap the pairs.

s: Moses went into the desert looking for God
he was at work, keeping his father-in-law's flock.
God calls to Moses after he turns aside to see
"when the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called unto him."
"the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed."

games.q: you're Moses, herding sheep, and a bush is burning but not burning up. what do you do?
o: turn aside and go see why.
run back to Jethro for help.
games.why: he turns aside to see, and only then does God call to him from the bush.

practice: If you can, take off your shoes, and socks too if you like, and stand, or sit with bare feet on the floor.
Feel what's under you, tile, carpet, wood, grass, and the weight moving through your heels and the balls of your feet: the ground you were already standing on.
If you pray, let the standing be your prayer; if not, let it be your attention.

wordCard.voice: Horeb. The mountain of God where Moses was told to take off his shoes, because the ordinary ground under his feet was holy. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: holy ground. The call came after Moses turned aside to see. Until tomorrow.
